title: Two hold a cloak (Bava Metzia 2a)
hookLine: two people claim one garment; each swears, and they divide it
tomorrow: A court that almost never executed

lines: I FOUND IT. I FOUND IT.
cards: One cloak, and two fists closed on it. Not tugging. Just holding.
One says: I found it, it's all mine. The other says: I found it, it's all mine. There are no witnesses, no receipt, and no window into either heart.
This is the case that opens the tractate Bava Metzia, the middle gate of the laws of damages and dealings. So what does a court do when both stories sound exactly the same?

teach.h: EACH SWEARS: NO LESS THAN HALF.
teach.b: Two hold a cloak. The Mishnah's ruling is short. Each one swears that they own no less than half of it, and they divide.
Look at what that oath does. Neither swears it's all theirs. Each swears only to the part that could be true for both at once.
The court doesn't pretend to know what it can't know. Then the Mishnah changes the case. One says, it's all mine.
The other says, half of it is mine. Now the first swears to no less than three quarters, the second to no less than a quarter.

teach.h: ALL VERSUS HALF: THREE QUARTERS, ONE QUARTER.
teach.b: The one claiming half has already granted the other half, so only one half is really in dispute, and only that half gets split. The rule isn't split everything down the middle.
It's split what's actually contested. The Talmud lingers over these few lines. One question it asks: if they're dividing anyway, why make anyone swear?
One answer: so that nobody grabs a stranger's cloak in the street, says it's mine, and hopes to walk off with half.

teach.h: THE OATH MAKES A GRAB COST SOMETHING.
teach.b: The oath makes a grab cost something. Read it once more and three pieces of a fair process show through.
Hear both sides as equals. Divide only what's truly in dispute. Make lying expensive.
And none of it depends on knowing who's right. A court that admits what it can't see.

how: Some students of the Talmud begin with Bava Metzia, whose opening case of two people holding one garment is studied line by line in yeshivas and study partnerships.

games.q: what does “two hold a cloak” mean?
o: a story of two brothers who shared one coat in winter
a rule that a found garment goes to whoever grabbed first
a case where two claim one find and each swears to half

games.q: the cloak case — tap the pairs.
p: each swears to half, and they divide
one says all, one says half

s: the court works out who really found the cloak
it can't know, so each swears to no less than half and they divide.
when one claims all and one claims half, they still split it evenly
only the disputed half is divided: three quarters and a quarter.
the Talmud says the oath is partly there to stop people grabbing cloaks
so that nobody seizes a stranger's garment and claims half of it.

games.q: you're the judge. one says the cloak is all theirs. the other says half of it is theirs. how do you divide it?
o: three quarters to the first, a quarter to the second.
all of it to the one who claims all.
games.why: the Mishnah gives three quarters and a quarter. the one claiming half has already granted the other half, so only one half is in dispute.

practice: Bring to mind one small dispute that's still open: whose turn it is, who said what, whose idea it was. Ask what the other person actually claims, and what each of you has already granted.
Find the piece that's truly contested, and notice how much smaller it is than the whole.

wordCard.voice: Two hold a cloak. The opening case of Bava Metzia: two claim one garment, each swears to no less than half, and they divide. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: two are holding a garment, the opening words of Bava Metzia.

carryVoice: Your line: each takes half. Fairness can start before anyone knows who's right. Go gently.
